title: Boss: it works on my machine
summary: Fix an app that is down from its curl error, ship a site with checksums, and write a health check.

steps.title: Support queue
body: Support queue. Three tickets about getting things from A to B: an app that is "down" (start from the curl error),
a site to ship and verify, and a health check the deploy pipeline can trust. The machine has no network, so the
services run on loopback and the "server" is a folder.

steps.title: The orders app is down
prompt: Ticket: *"`curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz` fails, and the orders page shows an error."* The app lives in `~/app`
(`server.py`, its settings in `app.env`, its log in `app.log`, and `start.sh` / `stop.sh`).
Start from the symptom: run the `curl`, read what it says, find the cause with `ss -tlnp` and the log, fix it, and
restart the app. Done means both of these answer **200**:

checks.name: /healthz answers 200 on port 8080
checks.fail: Nothing answers 200 on port 8080. `ss -tlnp` shows where the app listens; `app.env` decides it, and the app only reads it when it starts.

checks.name: /api/orders answers 200
checks.fail: `/api/orders` does not answer 200. `tail ~/app/app.log` shows the error behind the 500.

checks.name: only one copy of the app runs
checks.fail: There should be exactly one `server.py` running. Stop the old one (`~/app/stop.sh`) before starting again.

hints: `curl` says it could not connect: nothing listens on 8080. `ss -tlnp` shows the app on `127.0.0.1:8081`, and `app.env` says `PORT=8081`.
The log says `PermissionError` on `data/orders.json`. `ls -l ~/app/data` shows mode `000`: `chmod 644 ~/app/data/orders.json`.
explain: Read the symptom literally. *Could not connect* (connection refused) means nothing listens on that address and port:
check `ss -tlnp`. *Could not resolve host* is DNS. A timeout is usually a firewall or a dead route. An HTTP **5xx** means the
network is fine and the app is broken: read its log. Each one points at a different layer, so the first curl

steps.title: Ship a folder and prove it arrived intact
prompt: Ship the built site in `~/site` to the web server. This machine has no network, so the server's web root is the
folder `~/remote/srv/www` (on a real job this is `scp` or `rsync -a --delete` to another host).
1. Pack the site into `~/out/site.tar.gz`, **without** the `.cache` folder, with paths relative to the site (so that
`index.html` is at the top of the archive, not under `home/learner/site/`).
2. Write `~/out/SHA256SUMS` with a checksum line for every file in the site except `.cache`, with relative paths.
3. Unpack it so that `~/remote/srv/www/index.html` exists, and make the web root hold **exactly** the site's files

checks.name: the archive has the site, relative, without .cache
checks.cmd: tar tzf ~/out/site.tar.gz 2>/dev/null | sed "s#^\./##" | grep -qx index.html && ! tar tzf ~/out/site.tar.gz | grep -q "\.cache"
checks.fail: `tar tzf ~/out/site.tar.gz` should list `index.html` (or `./index.html`) at the top and nothing from `.cache`. `tar czf ~/out/site.tar.gz -C ~/site --exclude=.cache .` does both.

checks.name: the web root matches the site
checks.fail: The web root differs from the site (below): something is missing, extra (like `old.html`) or in the wrong folder.

checks.name: SHA256SUMS covers the site
checks.fail: `~/out/SHA256SUMS` should have one line for each of the 4 site files, without `.cache`.

checks.name: the checksums verify on the server
checks.fail: `sha256sum -c ~/out/SHA256SUMS`, run in `~/remote/srv/www`, does not pass. The paths in the file must be relative.

hints: `tar -C DIR` changes into DIR first, so `tar czf ~/out/site.tar.gz -C ~/site --exclude=.cache .` stores `./index.html`. Check with `tar tzf`.
Checksums with relative paths: `cd ~/site && find . -type f ! -path './.cache/*' -exec sha256sum {} + > ~/out/SHA256SUMS`.
Clear the web root, then unpack: `rm -rf ~/remote/srv/www/* && tar xzf ~/out/site.tar.gz -C ~/remote/srv/www`, then `cd ~/remote/srv/www && sha256sum -c ~/out/SHA256SUMS`.
explain: With a real host: `rsync -av --delete --exclude=.cache ~/site/ web1:/srv/www/` does steps 1 and 3 in one go, and only
sends what changed. The trailing slash on `site/` means "the contents of site"; without it you get `/srv/www/site/`.
Add `-n` (dry run) first when `--delete` is involved. Checksums are how you prove a release artifact is the one you
built, which is the same idea behind signed container images.

steps.title: A health check script with curl
prompt: After every deploy a job checks the endpoints in `~/urls.txt`. Write `~/bin/healthcheck FILE` that, for each URL in FILE:
- prints one line `CODE URL`, where CODE is the HTTP status (`curl -w '%{http_code}'` prints `000` when it cannot connect),
- gives each request at most 3 seconds,
and then exits **0** if every code was 2xx, **1** otherwise. Make it executable and try `~/bin/healthcheck ~/urls.txt`.

checks.name: it prints CODE URL for each line
checks.fail: The output does not match (diff below). One line per URL: the code, a space, the URL. A refused connection is `000`.

checks.name: it exits 1 when something is unhealthy
checks.fail: With a 503 and a refused connection in the list, the script should exit 1.

checks.name: it exits 0 when all is well
checks.cmd: f=$(mktemp); printf "%s\n" http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/orders > "$f"; ~/bin/healthcheck "$f" >/dev/null 2>&1; rc=$?; rm -f "$f"; test $rc = 0
checks.fail: With only healthy URLs, the script should exit 0.

hints: `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 3 URL` prints just the status. It exits non-zero when it cannot connect, so in a strict script add `|| true`.
Loop over the file: `while IFS= read -r url; do ... done < "$1"`. Remember failure in a variable: `ok=1` before, `ok=0` when a code does not start with 2.
`case $code in 2??) ;; *) ok=0 ;; esac`, and at the end `[ "$ok" = 1 ]`, so the script's exit code is that test's.
solution: # healthcheck FILE: prints "CODE URL" for every URL in FILE; exits 1 unless all are 2xx.
explain: `curl -f` alone turns HTTP errors into a non-zero exit, but hides the code; `-w '%{http_code}'` (and
`%{time_total}`, `%{remote_ip}`) tells you what happened. Always set `--max-time` (and `--connect-timeout`) in
scripts: without them a hanging server hangs your deploy. Kubernetes readiness probes and load balancer health
checks work the same way: a status code, a timeout, a threshold.
